prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its incretin action, and for the development of long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonists for the treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six openings put B041 first, but I do not take that as proof of merit. The merit is that this is a discrete discovery chain with a clear change in the field: proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, then GLP-1 as the active insulinotropic hormone, then the pharmacological problem of its short half-life, and finally long-acting agonists with demonstrated benefit in diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. The effect has been confirmed over more than a decade in independent randomized trials, so this is a mature result and not a fashion. Holst (human physiology), Drucker (GLP-1 and GLP-2 biology and translational rationale) and Knudsen (the acylation-based design behind liraglutide and semaglutide) cover the physiology, the therapeutic concept and the drug design as three distinct and defensible contributions.
statement.case_against: Credit is the weak point. Mojsov's identification of the biologically active GLP-1(7-36) form is a real contribution that a three-person limit forces us to leave out or trade against Knudsen, and Habener is not even among the credited names. A trio that includes an industrial drug-development scientist alongside two physiologists also invites the objection that we are rewarding a product and not a discovery. If the committee judges that the basic discovery is the Nobel-worthy part, then Drucker, Holst and Mojsov is the cleaner basic-science trio, and a drug-development component would need separate justification.

responses.point: Proposes Drucker, Holst and Mojsov as the strongest scientific trio, treating Knudsen's industrial development of liraglutide as a plausible alternative but not a core credit.
responses.response: I take this seriously and I do not think it is wrong on the science: identifying the active peptide form was a necessary step. But the prize is for a discovery that changed a field, and the change came from getting a stable, long-acting molecule into patients. Without Knudsen's design work the physiology would remain a mechanistic finding with modest clinical consequence. Where I would concede ground is that the evidence I have is only a summary of the credit dispute, and if the committee can show that Mojsov's contribution was decisive and independent of Habener's, I would reconsider which of the two takes the third place.

responses.point: Ranks BCR-ABL inhibition (B004) second, on the grounds of clean credit, over twenty years of survival data and a paradigm for kinase-inhibitor oncology, and ranks anti-TNF therapy (B022) third.
responses.response: I agree that B004 has the cleanest attribution of any candidate on this list, and its maturity is not in doubt. My reservation is about novelty of the prize as a statement: kinase-inhibitor oncology is a very large field, and I would want to see whether the committee is prepared to credit the compound discovery and the clinical proof together, since Lydon's role is easy to underweight. I keep it as a strong later-year candidate but not ahead of CAR-T or optogenetics this year. I did not rank anti-TNF in my top eight; it is a fair point that the maturity is excellent, but I would want the attribution among Feldmann, Maini and the antibody engineers to be looked at more closely before supporting it.

responses.point: Ranks antisense correction of SMN2 splicing (B007) third and proposes only June and Sadelain for CAR-T, treating Rosenberg as a foundational predecessor.
responses.response: The SMN2 case is attractive because the mechanism is clean and the clinical effect in spinal muscular atrophy is dramatic, and I accept that it is as mature as the other nominees. My reservation is that the field-wide change is narrower than for incretins or CAR-T, and nusinersen was developed by a small group, which makes it a good candidate for a later prize rather than for this year. On CAR-T I agree with a pair and not a trio: June and Sadelain have the direct claim on costimulated CAR design and clinical translation, while Rosenberg's adoptive transfer work is real but earlier and conceptually separate. That is a more disciplined reading than my own opening, and I would favour it if CAR-T becomes the prize.

responses.point: Like me, ranks GLP-1, CAR-T and optogenetics first through third, and notes that Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenboeck have strong claims so any three-person optogenetics split leaves out significant contributors.
responses.response: I agree on the order and I think the attribution problem for optogenetics is a more serious obstacle than the openings suggest: six credited names for three places means any choice is contestable, and Nagel, Hegemann and Deisseroth is only one defensible resolution. That is why I would hold optogenetics as a second alternative rather than propose a two-part prize with it this year. I do not see a reason to split the prize now, because GLP-1 can carry three names by itself.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen should hold the third place; the supplied material does not settle the credit dispute over GLP-1(7-36) and Habener is not available.
Whether a citation combining physiology and drug design is better than a two-part prize with a separate, distinct second achievement.
Whether the newest indications (cardiovascular, renal and neurological) need more follow-up before they feature in the citation.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted ballots. My nuclear-receptor co-authorship with Ronald Evans and my KI collaborations (Johan Ericson; Per Svenningsson and Abdel El Manira as colleagues) involve no shortlisted candidate. Dopamine-neuron research has no overlap with the incretin or other shortlisted topics.
